title: A/B Testing Platform
seoTitle: Design an A/B Testing Platform Like Optimizely
description: Design an experimentation platform — deterministic user bucketing, low-latency assignment, exposure logging, and computing statistically sound results.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is an A/B Testing Platform?
blocks.text: An experimentation platform lets product teams show different variants of a feature to different users — say, a green vs. blue checkout button — and measure which performs better on metrics like conversion.

items: Teams should be able to create an experiment with variants and traffic splits (e.g. 50/50).
Applications should be able to ask "which variant does this user see?" and get a consistent answer.
The platform should record which users were exposed to which variant.
Teams should see results: metric differences between variants with statistical significance.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Assignment adds negligible latency (< 5ms), ideally computed in-process.
Assignment is sticky: a user sees the same variant every time.
Exposure logging handles billions of events per day without slowing apps.
Results are statistically sound — no peeking bias, correct sample ratios.
**Experiment**: name, status, variants with traffic percentages, target audience, primary metrics.
**Assignment**: the variant a user gets for an experiment (computed, not stored).
**Metric event**: user actions (purchase, click) used to compute outcomes.

blocks.text: The **Experiment Service** stores experiment definitions and publishes a versioned **config snapshot** (all active experiments) to a CDN or config store.

The SDK downloads the config snapshot and refreshes it every few seconds. Assignment is **deterministic hashing**: `bucket = hash(experimentId + userId) % 10000`, mapped onto the variant ranges. No network call and no stored assignment table are needed, and the same user always lands in the same bucket.
When the application actually renders the variant, the SDK logs an exposure, batched asynchronously, so logging never blocks the request. Events flow through Kafka into a data warehouse.
A daily (or hourly) pipeline joins exposures with metric events per user, aggregates per variant, and computes effect sizes and confidence intervals.
1) How do we assign variants quickly and consistently?

approach.text: On first request, randomly pick a variant and store it in a database; read it on every request.

challenges.text: A database lookup on every feature check, and a huge assignments table.

approach.text: Hash `(experimentSalt, userId)` into buckets and map buckets to variants using the locally cached config. Changing the salt re-randomises a new experiment, so users aren't correlated across experiments. Ramping from 10% to 50% only adds buckets, so existing users keep their variant.

challenges.text: Changing variant weights mid-experiment reassigns users — the platform should block it or start a new version.

blocks.text: 2) How do we get trustworthy results?

items: Analyse only **exposed** users (those who actually saw a variant), not everyone assigned.
Check for **sample ratio mismatch**: if a 50/50 test shows 52/48, assignment or logging is broken and results can't be trusted.
Avoid peeking bias: fix the sample size in advance, or use sequential testing methods that allow continuous monitoring.
Reduce variance with techniques like CUPED (using pre-experiment behaviour) to reach significance with fewer users.

blocks.text: Running many overlapping experiments on the same surface can cause interactions. Use **layers**: experiments in the same layer are mutually exclusive, while different layers are independent.
3) How do we handle billions of exposure events?

Deduplicate in the SDK (log an exposure once per user per experiment per session), batch and compress events, and write through Kafka to a columnar warehouse partitioned by date and experiment. Results are computed with pre-aggregation per user before joining, which keeps queries tractable.

quiz.question: How can variant assignment be sticky without storing it?
options: Deterministic hashing of experiment salt and user ID
quiz.explanation: The same inputs always hash to the same bucket.

quiz.question: What does a sample ratio mismatch indicate?
options: Assignment or logging is broken, so results can't be trusted
quiz.explanation: A 50/50 test should show roughly equal exposures.

quiz.question: Why analyse only exposed users?
options: Assigned users who never saw the variant dilute the measured effect
quiz.explanation: Including unexposed users biases results toward zero.

quiz.question: Why shouldn't you repeatedly peek and stop when results look significant?
options: It inflates false positives unless sequential methods are used
quiz.explanation: Multiple looks increase the chance of a spurious win.
